enonce_intro_markdown:
**SECTION ONE: LOGIC**

**1.** *Read the passage below and answer the questions that follow:*

It was a hot day in C.S. Bom. It was about 12: noon when a man walked into the school with a machete and was looking for the senior boys' prefect. When asked what was wrong he said, it is either he kills the boy or he burns the school. The Principal immediately called the police. When the policemen came, the man said "If he is arrested, then he will burn the school upon his release and he will kill the senior boys' prefect. The Principal then told him that if he is willing to explain what is wrong then he will not be arrested. It was at this point that the man said the senior prefect had impregnated his daughter. The senior boys' prefect said he has never impregnated any girl so he cannot impregnate the man's child. Only illiterate parents are violent, said the vice principal.

**QUESTIONS**

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) Identify a Categorical statement from the passage and translate it into standard form. (2 marks)

(ii) State the contrary of a (i) above. (2 marks)

(iii) Given a (ii) above as True, what can be inferred of its Subaltern? (1 mark)

(iv) Determine the obverse of the subcontrary of a (iii) above. (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) A categorical statement from the passage, in standard form.**

A categorical statement relates two classes (a subject term and a predicate term) by a quantifier, a copula and a quality, and has one of the four standard forms A, E, I, O. The vice principal's remark *"Only illiterate parents are violent"* is such a statement (an **exclusive** proposition). The rule for exclusives is: *Only $S$ are $P$* means *All $P$ are $S$* (being $P$ is possible only for members of the class $S$).

> **All violent persons are illiterate parents.**

Quantifier: *All*; subject term: *violent persons*; copula: *are*; predicate term: *illiterate parents*. It is an **A proposition** (universal affirmative).

(Another categorical statement in the passage is the prefect's "he has never impregnated any girl", which gives the E proposition *No girls are persons impregnated by the senior boys' prefect*. The four steps below work in the same way with it; the A proposition is used here.)

**(ii) The contrary.**

The contrary of an A proposition is the **E** proposition with the same subject and predicate (same quantity, opposite quality):

> **No violent persons are illiterate parents.**

Contraries cannot both be true but can both be false.

**(iii) The subaltern of the contrary, given that the contrary is true.**

The subaltern of an E proposition is the **O** proposition with the same subject and predicate (same quality, opposite quantity): *Some violent persons are not illiterate parents.* On the traditional square of opposition, **truth passes down from the universal to the particular** (subalternation): if the E proposition is true, its subaltern is **true**.

> **Inference: "Some violent persons are not illiterate parents" is true.**

(This follows the traditional convention of the syllabus, which gives universal propositions existential import; in modern Boolean logic a true E does not guarantee a true O.)

**(iv) The obverse of the subcontrary of (iii).**

The proposition of (iii) is the O proposition. Its **subcontrary** is the **I** proposition with the same subject and predicate (both particular, opposite quality): *Some violent persons are illiterate parents.* (Given that the O proposition is true, the subcontrary is undetermined: subcontraries cannot both be false but may both be true.)

**Obversion** keeps the subject, changes the quality of the proposition (affirmative to negative) and replaces the predicate by its complement (term-complement). From I: *Some $S$ are $P$* we get O: *Some $S$ are not non-$P$*.

> **Some violent persons are not non-illiterate-parents.**

The obverse is logically equivalent to the I proposition it comes from, so it has the same truth value (undetermined here).

questions.enonce_markdown:
Using the terms: "politicians" as minor term, "lawyers" as middle term, and "cheats" as major term:

(i) Construct an AII-1 syllogism. (2 marks)

(ii) State the mood and figure of b (i) above. (1 mark)

(iii) Using the AII-1 syllogism in b (i) above, construct an Enthymeme of the Second Order. (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Let $P$ = cheats (major term), $M$ = lawyers (middle term), $S$ = politicians (minor term).

**(i) The AII-1 syllogism.**

In the **first figure** the middle term is the subject of the major premise and the predicate of the minor premise (pattern $M$-$P$, $S$-$M$, $S$-$P$). **A** gives the major premise, **I** the minor premise, **I** the conclusion:

> All lawyers are cheats. (major premise, A: *All $M$ are $P$*)
> Some politicians are lawyers. (minor premise, I: *Some $S$ are $M$*)
> Therefore, some politicians are cheats. (conclusion, I: *Some $S$ are $P$*)

The syllogism is valid (it is the mood **Darii**): the middle term is distributed in the major premise (subject of an A), no term is distributed in the conclusion that is undistributed in the premises, and the conclusion is particular as it must be when one premise is particular.

**(ii) Mood and figure.**

- **Mood: AII** (the types of the major premise, the minor premise and the conclusion).
- **Figure: 1** (the middle term is subject in the major premise and predicate in the minor premise).

The syllogism is therefore **AII-1** (Darii).

**(iii) An enthymeme of the second order.**

An enthymeme is a syllogism in which one proposition is left unexpressed. In the traditional classification, the **first order** suppresses the major premise, the **second order suppresses the minor premise**, and the third order suppresses the conclusion. Suppressing the minor premise "Some politicians are lawyers" gives:

> Some politicians are cheats, because all lawyers are cheats.

(Expressed: the major premise and the conclusion. Understood but not stated: *Some politicians are lawyers*.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) Identify an appropriate hypothetical proposition and use it to construct a Simple Destructive Dilemma. (3 marks)

(ii) Refute the dilemma in c (i) above by grasping between the horns. (3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Let $A$ = the man is arrested, $B$ = he burns the school upon his release, $K$ = he kills the senior boys' prefect.

**(i) A simple destructive dilemma.**

*The appropriate hypothetical proposition.* The man himself says in the passage: *"If he is arrested, then he will burn the school upon his release and he will kill the senior boys' prefect."* This is a conditional with one antecedent ($A$) and two consequents: $A \supset (B \cdot K)$, which gives the two conditionals $A \supset B$ and $A \supset K$ with the **same antecedent**.

A **simple** dilemma has a single, common antecedent in its conditional premise (and a single conclusion); it is **destructive** when the disjunctive premise **denies the consequents** and the conclusion denies the antecedent. Form: $(A \supset B) \cdot (A \supset K),\ \sim B \vee \sim K\ \therefore\ \sim A$.

> If the man is arrested, he will burn the school; and if the man is arrested, he will kill the senior boys' prefect.
> Either he will not burn the school or he will not kill the senior boys' prefect.
> Therefore, the man will not be arrested.

The argument is valid (checked with a truth table in Python: no assignment makes both premises true and the conclusion false). If $A$ were true, both $B$ and $K$ would follow, which the disjunctive premise rules out.

**(ii) Refuting the dilemma by grasping the horns.**

The **horns** of a dilemma are the conditional propositions of the major premise. To **grasp (take) the dilemma by the horns** is to **deny the conditional premise**: to show that the consequent does not really follow from the antecedent (at least one of the two conditionals is false).

For example: *It is not true that if the man is arrested he will burn the school or kill the prefect.* Arrest is followed by investigation, and possibly by a trial, a conviction and a prison sentence; the man's anger may subside once his complaint has been heard (the Principal has already offered him a hearing), and the school and the prefect can be protected by the police. Since the consequents do not necessarily follow from the arrest, the major premise is false or unproved, and the conclusion "he will not be arrested" is not established. The dilemma is refuted without questioning its validity: its form is valid, but its major premise is not true.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) Identify, explain and clearly illustrate the fallacy most clearly committed by the senior boy's prefect. (4 marks)

(ii) Why do we study Fallacies? (1 mark)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) The fallacy: begging the question (*petitio principii*, circular reasoning).**

*Identification.* The prefect says that he *"has never impregnated any girl"* and concludes that he *"cannot impregnate the man's child"*.

*Explanation.* **Begging the question** is committed when an argument assumes, openly or in disguise, the very point to be proved: the premise already contains (presupposes) the conclusion, so the argument proves nothing new. Here, the point at issue is whether the prefect impregnated *this* girl, the man's daughter. The premise "he has never impregnated any girl" is a universal denial that already covers the daughter, so it can be accepted only if the conclusion is already accepted. The reasoning goes in a circle: *he did not impregnate this girl because he never impregnated any girl*, and the only evidence that he never impregnated any girl would include that he did not impregnate this one. The passage also slides from "has never" (a matter of fact) to "cannot" (an impossibility).

*Illustration.* "The newspaper is reliable because it always tells the truth, and we know it always tells the truth because it is a reliable newspaper." (The same mistake: the premise is the conclusion in other words.) In the passage: a proper reply would give independent evidence (an alibi, a medical or DNA test, witnesses) instead of repeating the denial.

(The vice principal's remark "Only illiterate parents are violent" is also open to criticism, as a generalisation, but it is not the prefect's argument.)

**(ii) Why do we study fallacies?**

We study fallacies in order to **recognise and avoid errors of reasoning in our own arguments**, to **detect faulty arguments used by others** (in advertising, politics, quarrels, media) so as not to be misled by persuasion that is not based on good reasons, and thereby to **argue correctly and reach the truth**, which is the aim of critical thinking.
